content:
Hi all,

We've just made public 40 Lean libraries written by AI agents, as part of the Mathlib Initiative's Formal Frontier project. You can find them all at https://github.com/orgs/FormalFrontier/repositories

When we started the Formal Frontier project in April, the plan was to autoformalize a number of sources more or less completely. The state of autoformalization has changed significantly since then. Results that looked out of reach for AI not long ago now get formalized routinely, often several times over. With enough time and inference budget a single book is now within reach with off-the-shelf AI tools.

The overall goal of Formal Frontier hasn't changed. We want to provide formal libraries that become part of the wider ecosystem and are genuinely useful the community. With this in mind, we believe that formalizing one text at a time is no longer where we can add the most value. So we shifted our focus, and the libraries we're announcing here are our initial results.

The libraries come out of what we call the "Formal Frontier Hive." It's a new system we built over the last two months that keeps a team of AI agents collaborating and working continuously and autonomously to autoformalize content from a selection of texts. The libraries themselves are not tied to any particular source. A given library can contain content from many sources, and content from each source can contributes to many libraries. In particular, at this point we're not claiming any formalization coverage of any source.

We choose the sources and set the rules the agents work by, but otherwise we stay out of the way of the agents. The agents create the libraries, write and review the Lean code, manage the dependencies between libraries and prepare the releases. Right now they're working from the following small set of sources:

  • Neukirch-Schmidt-Wingberg's Cohomology of Number Fields,
  • Milne's Algebraic Groups,
  • Vakil's The Rising Sea,
  • Weibel's The K-book and
  • Fujiwara-Kato's Foundations of Rigid Geometry I.

The agents are also able to request access to additional auxiliary sources as part of their work, and they have already requested access to sources such as EGA/SGA and a proof of Hochster's Theorem.

We are planning to scale this system up in stages, both in the number of sources and in the number of agents working in the system. Long-term, we believe the Hive is a system that can scale massively, and the ultimate goal is to formalize all standard mathematical content.

I want to be clear that this is partly an experiment. We want to see whether a whole ecosystem of formal mathematics libraries can be developed and managed by AI agents autonomously. Writing Lean code that typechecks is only one part of that. The agents also have to ensure semantic alignment, decide how the mathematics gets split into libraries, review each other's work, keep the libraries compatible with each other, release them and maintain them over time.

Since the point is for these libraries to be reused and build on, any one of them is not tied to any particular source. The idea is that material shared by several books gets formalized once, in the library for that theory, and is reused from there. The approach we're using to making sure the libraries really are reusable is to essentially force the agents to reuse them. All the libraries depend on mathlib, but they can only depend on each other through released versions. The agents therefore have to build on their own libraries the same way anyone else would.

Here is an illustration explaining how these libraries currently depend on each other.

The system is live, and the agents are still working. So these libraries are going to keep changing. The intention is for them to grow in breadth and depth and to improve overall as time goes on. If you want to depend on one of these libraries, I'd suggest pinning to a commit.

To be completely up front, the content in these libraries is not absolutely perfect:

  • They grow out of the sources being formalized, so some libraries are lacking in content. For example, complex-analysis only has a few results so far and is by no means a comprehensive library of complex analysis.
  • Some results aren't stated the way mathlib would. For example, the hairy ball theorem in sphere-topology is correct, but it doesn't use mathlib's TangentSpace.
  • There's technical debt. For example, this file in continuous-group-cohomology bumps maxHeartbeats as high as 3000000 and turns off backward.isDefEq.respectTransparency for some proofs.
  • Small lemmas that fill gaps in mathlib end up scattered across the libraries. The issue of whether AI-generated content belongs in mathlib is under active discussion, and we will always respect the decisions of the mathlib maintainer team and community standards.
  • The documentation is inconsistent across libraries.
  • Bumping mathlib across the suite of libraries has not yet been exercised.

We do not plan to fix these by editing the code ourselves. Rather, we intend to gradually improve the agents' instructions and protocols so issues like these are addressed automatically in the future.

Feedback is very welcome, and we're happy to discuss any of this here on zulip.

and a proof of Hochster's Theorem.

Just checking that you know that Fangming Li (John) formalized Hochster (manually) as part of his PhD thesis.

Thanks Kevin, yes, I am aware. The agents asked for a source with the proof primarily because spectral spaces show up in the sources they're targeting, not necessarily because Hochster's theorem is a formalization target for them. And in general, the protocols are set up in such a way so that proper attribution should be given if (parts of) the existing formalization are used somehow.

Are there plans to integrate the formal frontiers libraries into tau ceti or something similar?

Also, I wonder how much does "the Hive" review each other? Do you (or rather a review bot) check for stuff like generality? Do you ever "look back" and check if some definition was the "right/most convenient one" for a Lean formalisation?

@Felix Pernegger we don't have any plans for integrating into TauCeti, but since TauCeti runs by volunteers running their own agents, there is nothing stopping others from contributing content from these libraries into TauCeti.

As for review, yes, there is extensive review conducted by the agents. What you see on github are the "releases", which are commits mirroring commits made to a release branch in an internal code forge (a self-hosted instance of forgejo in this case). The agents open and review PRs, branch protection rules ensure review from agents with independent context, and review is based on specific protocols. PRs go into a main branch, then releases are reviewed again before committing to a release branch (which then gets mirrored on github).

The agents also have complete autonomy to refactor and move around content between the libraries, again based on some set of protocols. The only thing that requires an operator is setting up mirroring for a new library when the agents decide to create one. Because of this we also have an internal "incubator" library which is a place where agents contribute (in the usual way) any content whose associated library onboarding is pending.

As you mentioned, the state of autoformalization is changing quickly. One of the aims listed on the MI page is "responsible autoformalization". Besides the clear technical bits (Comparator, etc.) it doesn't seem like there's an obvious consensus on what this means. Is there a working definition of what this means to the folks working on Formal Frontier, perhaps that might later evolve into a public set of guidelines? Has this shifted at all with model capabilities? (Not trying to lock you into any opinion, just interested in hearing initial thoughts.)

Hi Chris -- yes, I agree there is no consensus in the community. One of the concrete things we did very early on in the Formal Frontier project is to put out and promote #formalization.yaml which is now used by hundreds of public projects, it's integrated with palomar, etc. Perhaps the most concrete definition of "responsible" refers to things like attribution and provenance more generally. But of course there are many more concerns with autoformalization that haven't been addressed yet.

Chris Henson said:

One of the aims listed on the MI page is "responsible autoformalization". Besides the clear technical bits (Comparator, etc.) it doesn't seem like there's an obvious consensus on what this means.

My opinions do not represent Mathlib Initative or Formal Frontiers, but to me there are several important steps for a healthy autoformalization ecosystem:

  • Ensure all previous work is properly cited, especially work of humans.
  • Transparent documentation of what models and tools are used to produce each artifact.
  • Persistent monitoring to ensure good asymptotics (quality -> Mathlib as tokens_spent -> infinity)
  • Proactive collaboration with other formal libraries, especially Mathlib, towards shared standards.
  • Building open source tools for cultivating human understanding of the core mathematical content.
I endorse this message.

Can you remark more about the DevOps aspect of managing the agents? Is it via https://github.com/FormalFrontier/pod? Is the compute local to user machines, or runs in a cloud? If in the cloud, what is managing those machines?
No, pod is an old orchestrator developed by @Kim Morrison and it just so happens that the repo is under the FormalFrontier github org. It's unrelated to this project.

The hive system runs in a cluster in the cloud, and each agent gets its own container. We have an internal forgejo instance for code/PRs/issues, and an internal zulip instance for communication (for both AIs and humans). The agent runtime does nothing more than keep the agents alive, and we have been primarily using codex so far, although we're in the process of experimenting with alternative agent runtimes.

What cloud do you run on? Is forgejo also holding the agent code/runtime config, and is it self-synth/deploying? codex as a cli on a naked runtime? You're using issues/PRs as "crew" memory/task management, or is it convolved with the Zulip instance? Did you build any telemetry monitoring, agent self-improvement, or human facing dashboards as part of the infra? Is the infra code source available?

We're running on a kubernetes cluster (k3s to be precise) on hetzner. Our infra code is split into three repos: hive, which has the actual agent runtime code, the controller, etc.,ff-hive which is particular to the deployment of the agents in the cluter, and ff-stack which manages other components like forgejo, zulip, forgejo CI runners, etc. We do have a simple continuous deployment pipeline for ff-hive. hive is hosted on github, and is generic enough that I do expect it to be made public soon (it's still in flux, as I mentioned above, so not right away), but the other two are specific to our deployment so they will remain private.

Right now we're running codex with the daemon / app-server. There is a silly issue with codex if you want to change the developer instructions in the middle of a session which is forcing us to use the daemon. We're in the process of transitioning to using pi-durable since it has many benefits, including the fact that inference requests and responses can be stored in a central postgres database, and it allows for remote tool execution environments. Once that stabilizes, I will make the hive repo public.

One of the most important components of the system is indeed self-improvement. Each agent has a "charter" and "instructions" that get injected into its system prompt, but there is also an "operations" repo on forgejo which the agents manage themselves via PRs. Agents are instructed to collaborate on proposing and reviewing improvements to the overall system, coming up with strategies, etc., and these are preserved in the operations repo. Humans communicate with agents on the internal zulip server. The zulip server has dedicated channels like requests-to-agents where humans can make requests, and requests-to-operators where agents request things from humans. All of this is governed with natural language protocols in the operations repo.

Adam Topaz said:

As for review, yes, there is extensive review conducted by the agents. What you see on github are the "releases", which are commits mirroring commits made to a release branch in an internal code forge (a self-hosted instance of forgejo in this case). The agents open and review PRs, branch protection rules ensure review from agents with independent context, and review is based on specific protocols. PRs go into a main branch, then releases are reviewed again before committing to a release branch (which then gets mirrored on github).

I wonder what kind of quality mechanisms are in place. The protocols don't seem to be public like Tau Ceti rubrics yet (EDIT: reading the messages above again, it seems that the operations repo will be public when ready).

Also, based on Tau Ceti agent review experience, few rounds of reviews don't converge to an acceptable level of quality, leaving many refactors to be done with human attenton. So only one round (as the quoted reply seems to indicate) of independent review before release is likely insufficient.

Felix Pernegger said:

Are there plans to integrate the formal frontiers libraries into tau ceti or something similar?

I am also confused about the relation with Tau Ceti given that they both sponsored by the Mathlib Initiative and experiments in autoformalization. There are notably differences in approach, but given the result of both is basically AI authored lean library for some math subfields with some human steering, I can't tell if there are some notable dimensions (quality, time to completions, provenance?) in which we expect a difference.

It makes sense to me that formal frontiers and the community more broadly would perform different experiments at this point, even if there is overlap and duplication. There are different tradeoffs with speed and quality and level of human independence and self-consistency. This and Tau Ceti are experiments with libraries, prove2.me and lean eval are on the "bag of theorems" side.
(deleted)

There are no public plans about integrating Formal Frontier and Tau Ceti at this point, but it's something we are actively thinking about.

Tau Ceti is much more a "bazaar" style, i.e. anyone can contribute roadmaps, anyone can suggest changes to rubrics, and anyone can bring a worker agent to add content. This imposes various costs, but also lets use find resources to run it from many places.

(Formal Frontier is a program of the Mathlib Initiative, i.e. directly funded through MI and worked on by Adam and other MI staff. Tau Ceti is "incubated by" the Mathlib Initiative, which basically means that I talk to Johan and Adam a lot, but there's not actually any funding from the MI or dedicated staff time.)
